title: The Six Columns and the Iron Collar: Origen from Alexandria to Caesarea
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Alexandria, born into a Christian house
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No source gives a birth date. The year c. 185 is arrived at backward from Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.2.12, which says he was not quite seventeen when his father died in 202. Month and day are ordering devices. Coordinates are the Alexandria pin already in use in this corpus for the Brucheion and the Museion; the family's actual quarter is unknown.
stops.campa: Alexandria in the year the boy is born holds the largest Greek library in the world and the largest Jewish community outside Judaea, and a church that already teaches in the vocabulary of both. Leonides and his wife raise their eldest son inside that church. Nothing about the birth is recorded: no day, no month, no quarter of the city. The year itself is arrived at backward, from a sentence Eusebius writes a hundred and twenty years later saying the boy was not quite seventeen when his father died. Six more sons follow him.
suggested_refs: The Brucheion quarter of Roman Alexandria, seat of the Museion and the library

stops.name: Alexandria, the daily recitation
stops.date_confidence: attested as a practice, undated. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.2, describes the double curriculum without giving years. The date here orders the segment and is not a finding.
stops.campa: Leonides sets his son two curricula and lets neither displace the other. There is the ordinary Greek course an Alexandrian gentleman's son receives, grammar and rhetoric and the poets, the training that will later let him argue with philosophers in their own vocabulary. And there is scripture, committed to memory in passages and given back aloud, every day, before the Greek books are opened. The boy learns both as one thing, and is perhaps ten years old. Eusebius describes the arrangement without saying in what years it began or ended.
suggested_refs: The Greek grammatical curriculum of Roman Egypt, as reconstructed from the school papyri

stops.name: Alexandria, Leonides taken in the persecution
stops.date_confidence: attested to 202 (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.1-2). Month and day default to 01. The charge, the informer, and the length of the imprisonment are not given by any source.
stops.campa: The persecution under Septimius Severus reaches Alexandria and the authorities take Origen's father. Leonides is held in prison while the household waits. Eusebius does not say how long, or on whose information, or what was asked of him. The persecution is the emperor's business. What the record keeps instead is domestic: the eldest son, sixteen, is so determined to walk to the prison and be arrested alongside his father that nobody in the house can be trusted to leave a door unwatched.
suggested_refs: The Severan persecution at Alexandria, 202, known almost entirely from Eusebius

stops.name: Alexandria, the clothes hidden
stops.date_confidence: reported, not corroborated. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.2, is the sole witness; he claims access to letters and to people who knew Origen, but nothing independent confirms the episode. Month and day are ordering devices within 202.
stops.campa: His mother pleads with him and he does not listen. So she takes every article of his clothing out of the house and hides it, and the boy who wants to die for the faith finds he cannot walk out of his own room to do it. What he does instead is write. The letter he sends his father in prison survives as a single line quoted by Eusebius a century later, and the line is not consolation, and it is not a son asking for anything. He is telling a man with a wife and seven sons not to save himself for their sake.
stops.quote: Take heed not to change your mind on our account.
stops.quote_source: Origen to Leonides, quoted at Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.2, tr. NPNF2
suggested_refs: The lost letter of Origen to his imprisoned father, of which one clause survives

stops.name: Alexandria, the beheading and the confiscated estate
stops.date_confidence: attested to 202 (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.1-2; Jerome, De Viris Illustribus 54). The month and day are ordering devices; no source dates the execution more closely.
stops.campa: Leonides is beheaded. The estate goes to the imperial treasury, which is the ordinary legal consequence of the sentence and not an additional cruelty, and it leaves a widow with seven sons and no property in a city where property was what the family had. Origen is not quite seventeen. Eusebius reports the confiscation without comment, in the same breath as the execution. From here the household lives on other people's money, and every arrangement Origen makes for the next four years is an arrangement about how to eat.
suggested_refs: Roman bona damnatorum, the confiscation of a condemned man's estate to the fiscus

stops.name: Alexandria, the rich woman's household
stops.date_confidence: attested (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.2), dated only to the aftermath of the confiscation, so 202 or 203. The patroness is unnamed in every surviving source. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: A rich Alexandrian woman takes the martyr's son into her household and treats him, Eusebius says, as an adopted son. She is not named, here or anywhere else. She also keeps under her roof a teacher from Antioch called Paul, a man with a following in the city, and Origen accepts her bread and her lodging for years without once standing with the household when Paul leads it in prayer. He is seventeen and eating at the table of a patron whose theology he refuses. Neither of them, apparently, makes a scene about it.
suggested_refs: Paul of Antioch, the teacher whose prayers Origen would not join, otherwise unknown

stops.name: Alexandria, eighteen years old and the school entrusted
stops.date_confidence: attested to his eighteenth year (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.3). Two elements of the pool are corrected here. Eusebius VI.3.1 has him begin because persecution had driven every teacher out, while VI.3.8 says the school was entrusted to him alone by Demetrius: the appointment is the bishop's, not his own initiative, and Eusebius does not reconcile the two. Eusebius VI.3.3 also sets the persecution under the prefect Aquila, whose term in Egypt runs c. 206-211 and cannot be folded into a 203 date; that discrepancy is left open.
stops.campa: Persecution has emptied the city of anyone willing to teach the faith in public, so converts come to the martyr's son because there is nobody else. He instructs them. Bishop Demetrius, who presides over the church of Alexandria, then entrusts the catechetical school to him alone, and the appointment sticks: at eighteen he holds the teaching office of the largest Christian community in the Greek-speaking world. Eusebius gives both accounts, the vacuum and the appointment, a few paragraphs apart, and does not reconcile them.
suggested_refs: The Alexandrian catechetical school, whose institutional continuity from Pantaenus and Clement is disputed by modern scholarship

stops.name: Alexandria, the kiss at the door of the condemned
stops.date_confidence: attested for the persons and the practice (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.3-VI.5); the deaths are spread across the early years of the school and are not individually dated. The seven names are given here in full, correcting a pool list that omitted Basilides and the second Serenus.
stops.campa: Seven of his students go to their deaths, and Eusebius names them all: Plutarch first, then Serenus burned, Heraclides, Hero, a second Serenus beheaded, Herais who died still a catechumen, and Basilides counted seventh. Origen visits them in prison and walks with them to the court and to the killing ground, and at the door he salutes each of them with a kiss, in the open, where anyone can see it. It is the most exposed gesture available to a man already known in the city as a martyr's son. He makes it seven times.
suggested_refs: Basilides, the soldier converted by Potamiaena's execution, counted seventh in Eusebius's list

stops.name: Alexandria, the grammar school given up
stops.date_confidence: attested in sequence but not in year (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.3.8-9). The pool had him selling the books while teaching grammar and doing it to feed his mother and brothers; Eusebius has the two acts in the other order, the grammar school abandoned first, and frames the four obols as ascetic self-sufficiency, saying nothing about the family. Year, month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: With more students arriving than he can hold and the school formally his, he decides that teaching Greek grammar for a living is inconsistent with training men in divine subjects, and closes the grammar school. Then he sells his library, the classical texts he had been collecting since boyhood, to a buyer who agrees to pay him four obols a day for as long as he lives. Four obols is a labourer's floor. Eusebius presents the arrangement as self-sufficiency rather than as support for his mother and six brothers, and says nothing at all about how they ate.
suggested_refs: The obol and the daily wage in Roman Egypt, from the Oxyrhynchus accounts

stops.name: Alexandria, the floor, the bare feet, no wine
stops.date_confidence: attested as a sustained practice, undated (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.3). The year orders the segment. Eusebius's judgement that the regime endangered his health is his own, offered as praise.
stops.campa: The regime he sets himself is deliberate, and Eusebius records it with alarm: fasting carried past what any rule requires, sleep taken on the bare floor and cut short, no wine, no shoes, a single garment worn through several winters. He lives this way for years while lecturing every day and taking new students. Eusebius, who admires him, states without hedging that it endangered his health, and that he kept it up anyway. Nobody in Alexandria is recorded as having tried to talk him out of it, and the school went on filling all the while.
suggested_refs: Third-century Christian askesis before monasticism, of which this is among the earliest detailed descriptions

stops.name: Alexandria, the deed Eusebius calls daring
stops.date_confidence: reported and disputed. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.8, is the sole ancient witness; since the early twentieth century a substantial body of scholarship has questioned whether the self-castration happened at all, reading it as hostile tradition Eusebius passed on. Trigg accepts it, Chadwick and McGuckin doubt it. Origen's own Commentary on Matthew rejects a literal reading of the verse. The pool tagged this attested in one lens and reported in another; it is treated here as reported. Year, month and day are ordering devices within c. 206-213.
stops.campa: Eusebius sets the passage under a heading of his own devising, Origen's Daring Deed, and calls it evidence of an immature and youthful mind that at the same time gave the highest proof of faith and continence. The act was done in secret. Demetrius, on learning of it, admired greatly the daring nature of the act, and years afterwards used it against him in front of other bishops. Origen's own commentary on Matthew, written as an old man, rejects the literal reading of that verse outright. No other ancient writer reports the act, and scholarship since 1900 has widely doubted that it happened.
stops.quote: For he took the words, 'There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven's sake,' in too literal and extreme a sense.
stops.quote_source: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.8.1, tr. NPNF2
sources: Wikipedia, 'Origen', on twentieth-century doubts about the episode's historicity
suggested_refs: Origen, Commentary on Matthew XV.1-5, which argues against the literal reading of Matthew 19:12
Bodleian MS. Douce 195, a fifteenth-century illumination of the scene

stops.name: Alexandria, Heraclas takes the beginners
stops.date_confidence: the delegation to Heraclas is attested (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.15). The philosophy studies under a teacher named Ammonius and the philosopher's cloak reach Eusebius only inside a passage he quotes from the hostile pagan Porphyry at VI.19.5-8 and then argues against, so they are reported, not attested. The identification of this Ammonius with Ammonius Saccas, later teacher of Plotinus, is disputed and unresolved; Eusebius answers Porphyry by insisting that Ammonius was a Christian raised by Christian parents, which Porphyry denied, and neither claim is independently testable. Year, month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: The school has grown past one man. He hands the elementary instruction to Heraclas, a former pupil, and keeps the advanced students for himself, the ones who arrive with philosophy already in them and questions the catechism does not answer. To meet them he goes back to school himself, under a teacher named Ammonius, and puts on the philosopher's cloak. That last detail comes down only inside a passage Eusebius quotes from a pagan enemy in order to contradict it. He preserves the sentence and argues with everything standing around it.
stops.quote: When I devoted myself to the word, and the fame of my proficiency went abroad, and when heretics and persons conversant with Grecian learning, and particularly with philosophy, came to me, it seemed necessary that I should examine the doctrines of the heretics, and what the philosophers say concerning the truth.
stops.quote_source: Origen, from his own epistle, quoted at Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.19, tr. NPNF2
sources: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.15 and VI.19 (newadvent.org/fathers/250106.htm)
suggested_refs: Porphyry, Against the Christians, book III, surviving only in Eusebius's quotation of it

stops.name: Rome, to see the oldest church there is
stops.date_confidence: attested to the episcopate of Zephyrinus, who died in 217, so c. 212-215 (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.14.10). Month and day are ordering devices. Coordinates are the Rome pin already in use in this corpus. No building, meeting, or Roman contact is named by any source.
stops.campa: He crosses the Mediterranean for no business anyone recorded. Eusebius gives the reason in a clause he says came from Origen's own writing, and it is a scholar's reason: he wanted to see the oldest church there was. Nothing is said of whom he met. Hippolytus was preaching in Rome in those years and no source puts the two of them in a room. He stays briefly and sails back to Egypt, and the visit leaves no trace on the Roman side at all. Eusebius, in the same sentence, lets slip the other name people used for him, Adamantius.
stops.quote: Adamantius, for this also was a name of Origen, when Zephyrinus was bishop of Rome, visited Rome, desiring, as he himself somewhere says, to see the most ancient church of Rome.
stops.quote_source: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.14, tr. NPNF2
suggested_refs: The Roman church under Zephyrinus and Callistus, and the quarrel with Hippolytus that Origen's visit does not mention

stops.name: Bostra, the governor's soldier and the letters
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.19, reports the summons, the escort, and the return, and names neither the governor, the purpose, nor the town. Bostra is inferred as the seat of the Roman governor of Arabia and is not attested for this visit. The date c. 214-216 comes from the surrounding narrative and is not fixed by any source.
stops.campa: A soldier arrives in Alexandria carrying letters from the governor of Roman Arabia, addressed both to Bishop Demetrius and to the Roman prefect of Egypt, requesting that Origen be sent to him for a private interview. Both authorities release him and he goes. Eusebius records that he travelled under escort and that he came back. He does not record what the governor wanted, or what was said, or where in the province the two men met. Bostra is the provincial seat and the likeliest room, and no source puts him in it.
suggested_refs: Bostra, capital of the province of Arabia Petraea, and its Roman governor's residence

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, the layman told to preach
stops.date_confidence: attested for the preaching and the objection (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.19.16-17); the flight from Alexandria is reconstruction, since Eusebius reports the disturbances without naming Caracalla, and the connection to his punitive action against the city's youth is the modern reading. Dated 215/216 in the sources; month and day default within it. Coordinates are the Caesarea Maritima pin already in use in this corpus.
stops.campa: Alexandria goes up in violence, in trouble usually connected with Caracalla's punishment of the city's youth, and Origen leaves Egypt for the Palestinian coast. Theoctistus of Caesarea and Alexander of Jerusalem ask him to expound scripture publicly, in church, in front of them. He is a layman. Demetrius writes from Alexandria that this has never been heard of anywhere, a layman preaching in the presence of bishops, and sends deacons to bring him home. The two Palestinian bishops answer with precedents. He obeys the summons.
suggested_refs: Caracalla's reprisal at Alexandria, 215/216, reported by Cassius Dio
The exchange of letters between Demetrius and the Palestinian bishops, known only from Eusebius

stops.name: Alexandria, recalled by the deacons
stops.date_confidence: attested (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.19), dated only by position in the narrative. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: He comes back and picks the school up where he left it. Nothing in Eusebius suggests a punishment, a public reckoning, or any change in his standing; the deacons brought him home and the work resumed. Fourteen more Alexandrian years follow. But the question raised on the Palestinian coast, whether a bishop's permission is what makes a man fit to expound scripture in church, has now been asked aloud by both sides, and neither side has withdrawn its answer. It will be asked again, in the same province, by the same two bishops.
suggested_refs: The disputed boundary between the teaching office and the priesthood in the third-century church

stops.name: Alexandria, Ambrose brought out of Valentinus
stops.date_confidence: attested (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.18.1 for the conversion from Valentinianism, VI.23.2 for the writing apparatus). The pool cited VI.21 for both, which is the chapter on Julia Mamaea; that citation is corrected here. The year is a position in the narrative, not a date in any source.
stops.campa: Ambrose is a wealthy Alexandrian holding the teaching of Valentinus when Origen argues him out of it. What he does with the conversion is not to preach but to pay. From then on he is patron and pressure at once, commissioning, questioning, refusing to let a project lie unfinished, and the word that attaches to him in the sources is taskmaster. Nearly everything of Origen's that survives in any form exists because Ambrose decided to fund the copying of it. Eusebius names the conversion in one chapter of his sixth book and the money in another.
sources: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.18 and VI.23 (newadvent.org/fathers/250106.htm)
suggested_refs: Heracleon and the Valentinian school at Alexandria, the milieu Ambrose left

stops.name: Alexandria, more than seven amanuenses
stops.date_confidence: attested for the arrangement (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.23.2: 'he dictated to more than seven amanuenses, who relieved each other at appointed times'). The year is an ordering device. The Galatians discrepancy is from Roger Pearse's edited translation of Jerome's catalogue and its use of Crouzel's notes.
stops.campa: The method is industrial. He dictates; more than seven shorthand writers take him down in relays, relieved at appointed times; copyists work the shorthand up into fair text. Ambrose pays for all of it. No Christian before him has produced at anything like this rate. The catalogue Jerome later draws up from the library at Caesarea runs to hundreds of titles and does not agree with the manuscripts that survive: fifteen books on Galatians in Jerome's list against five attested elsewhere. The mouth is the instrument. The hand belongs to someone else.
sources: Roger Pearse, 'A List of the Works of Origen (Jerome, Letter 33)' (roger-pearse.com/weblog/2014/02/08/)
suggested_refs: Jerome, Letter 33, the catalogue of Origen's works drawn from the Caesarean library
The von der Goltz codex, against which Jerome's book-counts can be checked

stops.name: Antioch, the empress's escort
stops.date_confidence: contested and not resolved. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.21, places the summons in the reign of Severus Alexander and calls Mamaea the mother of the emperor, which rules out anything before March 222; the pool's window of c. 218-222 falls in Elagabalus's reign and is rejected here. Many reconstructions put the Antioch summons at c. 231-232, when Alexander was at Antioch for the Persian campaign, which would place it after the break with Demetrius, whereas Eusebius has him return to Alexandria afterwards. The date given here follows Eusebius's narrative position and is an ordering device, not a finding. Coordinates are the Antioch on the Orontes pin already in use in this corpus.
stops.campa: Julia Avita Mamaea, mother of the emperor Severus Alexander, is staying at Antioch and sends for the Alexandrian teacher under military escort. Soldiers are detailed to bring a private schoolmaster up the coast because an emperor's mother wants to ask him something. He stays with her while she is in the city and explains the Christian teaching to a woman with real influence over her son's court. Eusebius calls her religious and does not claim she converted. No content of the conversation survives. Then he goes home to Egypt.
suggested_refs: Julia Avita Mamaea and the religious policy of the court of Severus Alexander

stops.name: Alexandria, the columns set side by side
stops.date_confidence: attested for the arrangement and the named versions (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.16, which describes the parallel columns with the Hebrew text and names Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion, and mentions the fifth, sixth and seventh versions of the Psalms). The second column of Greek transliteration, carried by the pool, is not in Eusebius and rests on later witnesses such as Epiphanius and the Milan palimpsest; it is omitted here. The work spans decades and both cities; the year is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The project is a book nobody could lift. He sets the Hebrew of the Old Testament beside the Greek of Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and the Septuagint, arranged in parallel columns so that a reader can see at a glance where the churches' Greek and the synagogues' Hebrew part company. For the Psalms he adds a fifth version, a sixth, and a seventh. He is doing to scripture what Alexandrian grammarians had done to Homer for four hundred years, and he is the first to do it to this text. It was too large ever to be copied entire, and no complete copy survived.
suggested_refs: The Milan Hexapla palimpsest, Ambrosiana O 39 sup., the largest surviving witness to the columns
Alexandrian Homeric textual criticism from Zenodotus to Aristarchus

stops.name: Alexandria, the Commentary on John against Heracleon
stops.date_confidence: attested (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.24: the first five books of the John commentary, the first eight on Genesis, Psalms 1-25, Lamentations, two books On the Resurrection and the Stromateis all written at Alexandria). The pool over-hedged this as reconstruction with no citation; the citation exists and is given. The Heracleon target comes from Origen's own commentary, not from Eusebius. Year, month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: He begins the commentary on John at Ambrose's request and writes five books of it before leaving Egypt. It is aimed at Heracleon, the Valentinian who had commented on the same gospel first, and it argues line by line rather than by denunciation, quoting the opponent at length before answering him. Heracleon survives today almost entirely inside Origen's refutation of him. From the same Alexandrian years come the first eight books on Genesis, commentaries on Psalms 1 to 25 and on Lamentations, two books on the resurrection, and the Stromateis.
sources: Origen, Commentary on John, books I-V
suggested_refs: The surviving fragments of Heracleon's commentary on John, preserved only by his refuter

stops.name: Alexandria, On First Principles
stops.date_confidence: attested to the Alexandrian years (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.24). The Greek is substantially lost; the four books survive mainly in Rufinus of Aquileia's Latin of c. 397-398, made by a translator who stated openly that he corrected passages he took to be later heretical insertions, and Jerome's rival literal Latin version, produced to expose those changes, is itself lost. No modern edition can adjudicate between them. Year, month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: He writes the first systematic Christian theology anyone attempts: four books on God, on the rational creatures, on the world, and on scripture, argued the way a philosopher argues, with the matters he takes to be settled by the apostolic teaching marked off from the matters he takes to be open. That distinction is the design of the whole book. It is also the distinction his accusers will not grant him. The Greek is lost. What survives is a Latin version made a century and a half after his death by a translator who admitted cutting what he judged to be other men's heresies out of it.
stops.quote: The teaching of the Church, transmitted in orderly succession from the apostles, and remaining in the Churches to the present day, is still preserved.
stops.quote_source: Origen, De Principiis, Preface, tr. ANF vol. 4
sources: Roger Pearse, 'A List of the Works of Origen (Jerome, Letter 33)' (roger-pearse.com/weblog/2014/02/08/)
suggested_refs: Rufinus of Aquileia's Latin De Principiis, c. 397-398, and his preface defending the cuts
The Philocalia of Origen, a fourth-century anthology attributed to Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus, which preserves Greek that Rufinus's Latin otherwise replaces

stops.name: Achaea, sent to Greece on the church's business
stops.date_confidence: partly mis-sourced in the pool and corrected here. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.23.4, says only that he was sent to Greece on account of a pressing necessity in church matters, and names neither Achaea, nor Corinth, nor any doctrinal dispute. The Achaean heresy detail comes from Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 118, reporting Pamphilus's lost Apology. The coordinate is Ancient Corinth, chosen as the province's principal see, and the arrival there is not narrated in any source. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: The church sends him to Greece on what Eusebius calls a pressing necessity in church matters, and declines to say what the necessity was. Later writers fill in a heresy in Achaea that needed answering, and the filling-in comes from Photius reading a lost defence of Origen, not from Eusebius. What matters about the errand is the route. He travels overland through Palestine, and the road takes him past two bishops who have wanted for fifteen years to put their hands on his head. He is forty-five and still a layman.
sources: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 118, summarising Pamphilus's Apology for Origen
suggested_refs: Pamphilus of Caesarea's Apology for Origen, surviving in Rufinus's Latin of book I and in Photius's summary

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, the hands laid on a layman from Egypt
stops.date_confidence: attested (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.23.4; Jerome, De Viris Illustribus 54; Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Origen and Origenism'), dated c. 230-231; month and day are ordering devices. Whether the ordination was a courtesy or a deliberate provocation is asserted in opposite directions by partisan sources and is not resolved here.
stops.campa: Theoctistus of Caesarea and Alexander of Jerusalem ordain him presbyter as he passes through, in their own province, without asking the bishop of Alexandria. Whether that is a courtesy long overdue or a raid on another see's most famous man depends on which account you read, and the accounts were written by partisans of opposite sides. Demetrius has presided over Alexandria for four decades and now holds a charge he can bring in canonical language rather than in the language of jealousy. The ordination is valid where it was performed.
suggested_refs: The canonical rule against ordaining a cleric outside his own bishop's jurisdiction, later fixed at Nicaea

stops.name: Alexandria, the synods and the deposition
stops.date_confidence: reported, not attested, and re-sourced against the pool. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.26, contains no synod, no expulsion and no deposition; its content is the move to Caesarea, Demetrius's death after forty-three years as bishop, and Heraclas's succession. The two Alexandrian synods come from Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 118, echoed by Jerome, and the decrees themselves do not survive. Eusebius's attribution of jealousy to Demetrius is his own partisan reading. Month and day are ordering devices within 231/232.
stops.campa: Demetrius calls a synod, which bars Origen from teaching in Alexandria and orders him out of the city; a second assembly afterwards strips him of the priesthood he has just been given. The decrees do not survive. What comes down is Photius's summary of a lost defence, Jerome's echo of it, and Eusebius's silence, which is loud, since his sixth book skips the synods entirely. Palestine, Arabia, Phoenicia and Achaea decline to recognise the sentence. Demetrius dies soon after, in his forty-third year as bishop, and Heraclas takes the chair and does not recall his old teacher.
suggested_refs: The lost acts of the Alexandrian synods of 231/232, known only at second and third hand

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, quitting Egypt
stops.date_confidence: attested for the permanent removal (Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Origen and Origenism'; Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.26 for the move in Alexander's tenth year). Dated 231/232; month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: He leaves Egypt and does not return to it. Caesarea is a harbour town with a Greek theatre, an aqueduct and a governor's residence, the seat of the Roman administration of Palestine, and it is two provinces away from the man who deposed him. He is about forty-seven, a priest in Palestine and a deposed layman in Egypt, and he will live the remaining twenty years in the first of those two conditions. Everything of his that anyone still reads whole was either written here or finished here.
suggested_refs: The library of Caesarea, built around Origen's books and catalogued by Pamphilus and Eusebius

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, two brothers who never reach the law school
stops.date_confidence: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.30, names Theodore, later Gregory, and his brother Athenodore, and supplies neither the five-year figure nor the abandoned law studies at Berytus; both of those come from Gregory's own Address of Thanksgiving to Origen, and the five years are independently reported by the Catholic Encyclopedia. The pool's two lenses gave c. 232-235 and c. 233-238; the later window is preferred here, since a five-year course beginning in the very year Origen arrived is the weaker reconstruction. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Two brothers from Pontus, headed for the law schools at Berytus down the coast, stop at Caesarea and never get there. They stay about five years. Gregory's farewell oration describes the method from inside: the master begins with dialectic and the sciences, moves to ethics, works through the philosophers of every school except the ones who deny providence, and only then opens scripture, on the argument that a man who cannot reason will misread it. Gregory goes home to Pontus and becomes a bishop there.
stops.quote: I wish to ask you to extract from the philosophy of the Greeks what may serve as a course of study or a preparation for Christianity.
stops.quote_source: Origen, Letter to Gregory Thaumaturgus, tr. ANF vol. 4
sources: Gregory Thaumaturgus, Address of Thanksgiving to Origen
suggested_refs: Gregory Thaumaturgus, Address of Thanksgiving to Origen, the only ancient description of the curriculum from a student's side

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, the other Caesarea
stops.date_confidence: reported. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.27, attests the friendship with Firmilian and mutual visits between the two men in general terms and dates none of them. Placing Origen physically in Cappadocia through the Maximinus persecution is a modern reconstruction on thin evidence, and his whereabouts in 235-238 are not recoverable. Coordinates are Kayseri. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Firmilian, bishop of the other Caesarea, the inland one in Cappadocia, is a correspondent and an admirer, and Eusebius says the two men went back and forth between their cities. Some reconstructions put Origen in Cappadocia in hiding for the whole of the Maximinus persecution. Eusebius attests the friendship and the visits only in the most general terms and dates none of them. He is somewhere between two Caesareas in those years, and the record does not say which.
suggested_refs: Firmilian of Caesarea in Cappadocia, whose one surviving letter is preserved in Cyprian's correspondence

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, the Exhortation to Martyrdom
stops.date_confidence: attested for the treatise and its two dedicatees (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.28), dated to the persecution under Maximinus, 235-238. Origen's own whereabouts during those years are uncertain. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Maximinus Thrax comes to power by killing his predecessor and moves against the household and the churchmen of the murdered emperor's circle. Ambrose and Protoctetus, a presbyter of Caesarea, both suffer unusual hardships in it, and Origen writes them a treatise. It is not consolation. It argues that the confession made in front of a magistrate completes what baptism began, and that a man who has agreed to die must not then bargain. It is written by someone who at sixteen had to be kept indoors by force to stop him doing exactly that. Neither Ambrose nor Protoctetus is executed.
suggested_refs: Origen, Exhortation to Martyrdom, addressed to Ambrose and Protoctetus

stops.name: Athens, the Ezekiel finished and the Song begun
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The pool carries this from a synthesis of Eusebius and Jerome's catalogue and did not re-fetch a passage for it; no source reached in this pass narrates the Athenian stay directly. The date window c. 238-244 is inherited from that synthesis. Month and day are ordering devices. Who invited him and how long he stayed are not recorded anywhere.
stops.campa: He is in Athens long enough to work, and he works on two books at once, finishing the commentary on Ezekiel there and beginning the commentary on the Song of Songs, which he will complete at Caesarea in ten books. The Song is a sequence of love poems that never once mentions God, and he reads it as the courtship of the soul by the Word, at ten books' length, which is longer than the poems. What he was doing in Athens otherwise, who brought him there, and how long he stayed, no source says.
sources: Jerome, catalogue of Origen's works (Letter 33), as summarised by Roger Pearse (roger-pearse.com/weblog/2014/02/08/)
suggested_refs: Origen, Commentary on the Song of Songs, surviving in Rufinus's Latin of the prologue and first three books

stops.name: Bostra, Beryllus talked back
stops.date_confidence: attested (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.33; the pool's chronology lens cited VI.27, which is the Firmilian chapter, and that citation is corrected here). Dated to the reign of Gordian III, c. 238-244; month and day are ordering devices. The record of the discussion existed in Eusebius's day and does not survive.
stops.campa: Beryllus, bishop of Bostra, is teaching that Christ had no distinct divinity of his own before the incarnation, and the bishops of Arabia cannot move him. They send for Origen. Eusebius has it that Origen first got Beryllus to state clearly what he actually held, which nobody else had managed, and then reasoned with him until he changed it. It is the method Gregory had described from the classroom, cross-examination first and refutation afterwards. A written record of the discussion existed in Eusebius's day and does not now. Beryllus stayed a bishop.
suggested_refs: The lost acts of the synod of Bostra, seen by Eusebius and by nobody since

stops.name: Roman Arabia, the synod on the soul that dies
stops.date_confidence: attested for the synod and its outcome (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.37), which names no town; Bostra is used here as the likeliest Arabian see given the Beryllus precedent, and is not attested for this meeting. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: A second Arabian assembly, its town unnamed in Eusebius, is holding that the human soul dies with the body and is made again at the resurrection. Origen is called in a second time, argues against it, and Eusebius says the assembly changed its opinion. He is the church's expert witness on the nature of the soul. Three centuries later the doctrine of the soul that gets him condemned by name sits at the other end of the same question: that souls existed before their bodies were made.
suggested_refs: Third-century Arabian church councils, known only from Eusebius's summaries

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, the letter to Africanus on Susanna
stops.date_confidence: attested (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.31; both letters survive). Dated c. 240 in the pool; the year here is an ordering device within the Caesarean period. Africanus wrote from Alexandria.
stops.campa: Julius Africanus writes to say that the story of Susanna in the book of Daniel is spurious and fictitious and ought not to be read as scripture. Origen answers at length, defending the passage on the ground that it is what the churches actually read, and closes by asking pardon for his little ability and the little time he had. Two learned men disagree in writing about whether a text belongs in the Bible, neither of them appeals to an authority to settle it, and both letters survive.
stops.quote: Your letter, from which I learn what you think of the Susanna in the Book of Daniel, which is used in the Churches.
stops.quote_source: Origen, Letter to Africanus, tr. ANF vol. 4
suggested_refs: Julius Africanus, Chronographiae, and his letter on Susanna

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, the shorthand writers admitted
stops.date_confidence: attested (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.36: past the age of sixty he permitted stenographers to record his public discourses for the first time, and the twenty-five books on Matthew belong to this period). The Mount Tabor identification is credited to Origen in Eusebius and is already carried on apostle_peter.journey.json; Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.1, cites Origen for Peter's inverted crucifixion without naming which work. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Past sixty, he lets stenographers into his sermons for the first time, and what had been spoken and lost begins to be published. The homilies come down from this decision. So do the twenty-five books on Matthew, where he settles the unnamed high mountain of the Transfiguration as Tabor, a reading every pilgrim after him inherits. Elsewhere, in a work Eusebius quotes without naming it fully, he reports that Peter asked to be crucified head downward. Asked who wrote the letter to the Hebrews, which the churches read under Paul's name, he declines to decide.
stops.quote: But who wrote the epistle, in truth, God knows.
stops.quote_source: Origen, quoted at Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI, tr. NPNF2
sources: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.1, citing Origen on Peter
apostle_peter.journey.json, Mount Tabor and Circus of Nero stops
suggested_refs: Origen's homilies as taken down by the Caesarean stenographers, the bulk of them surviving only in Latin translation

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, a bishop cross-examined in public
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and re-sourced against the pool, which cited Eusebius. Eusebius nowhere mentions the Dialogue with Heraclides: the text was entirely unknown before the Tura discovery of August 1941 and was published by Jean Scherer as Entretien d'Origene avec Heraclide. Its Caesarean setting and its date within the 240s are scholarly placements, not attestations. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: A bishop named Heraclides has said something about the Father and the Son that his fellow bishops want examined, and Origen is brought in to question him in front of the assembly. A shorthand writer takes the whole session down: the questions, the answers, a bishop conceding a point in public, the room moving on to the next thing. Then the transcript disappears for seventeen centuries. It comes back in August 1941, in a stack of papyrus codices turned up by workmen clearing a quarry tunnel south of Cairo.
sources: Jean Scherer, Entretien d'Origene avec Heraclide (Tura papyri publication)
suggested_refs: Origen, Dialogue with Heraclides, the only surviving stenographic record of a third-century church debate

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, Against Celsus
stops.date_confidence: attested (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.36) for the eight books answering Celsus's True Discourse, written at Ambrose's urging. The remark on the near-extinction of Simon Magus's followers is carried from simon_magus.journey.json, which flags its own Origen citation as taken from a research pool and not independently re-fetched; it is unverified here and is stated as such. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Ambrose puts in front of him a book seventy years old by a pagan philosopher named Celsus and asks for an answer. Origen answers in eight books, and answers the way he answered Heracleon, by quoting his opponent almost entire and then taking the quotations one at a time. Celsus's True Discourse is lost. It exists today only because the man refuting it copied out so much of it that most of the attack can be reconstructed from inside the defence. Among the things he takes up is how few followers of Simon Magus are left anywhere in the world.
stops.quote: And this diviner method is called by the apostle the manifestation of the Spirit and of power.
stops.quote_source: Origen, Against Celsus I.2, tr. ANF vol. 4
suggested_refs: Celsus, The True Discourse, reconstructible only from the quotations in Origen's refutation

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, the letters to Philip and Severa
stops.date_confidence: attested that the letters existed (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.36); their contents are lost and no source quotes them. Eusebius does not say Philip was a Christian, and that inference goes beyond the text. Dated c. 244-249; month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: He writes to the emperor Philip and to Philip's wife Severa. Eusebius saw the letters and says so. Nobody since has seen them, and nothing of their contents is quoted by anyone. A rumour that Philip was himself a Christian circulated later, and Eusebius does not assert it here. A man expelled from his own church twenty years earlier is corresponding with the imperial house, and what passed between them is gone. Eusebius, who held both letters in his hands and could have summarised them, did not.
suggested_refs: Philip the Arab and the third-century tradition of a Christian emperor before Constantine

stops.name: Roman Palestine, the stocks at the fourth hole
stops.date_confidence: attested (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI.39), who drew the details from Origen's own letters. The exact city of the imprisonment is not named; Caesarea is presumed as his residence at the time rather than confirmed as the site of arrest, and the coordinate is the Caesarea Maritima pin already in use in this corpus. No court transcript or sentence survives. Month and day are ordering devices within 250-251.
stops.campa: Decius orders every subject of the empire to sacrifice and to produce a certificate for it. Origen is arrested. Eusebius, who had his letters, lists what was done to him: bonds, bodily tortures, torments under an iron collar, and confinement in the stocks for many days with his feet stretched to the fourth hole, under the threat of fire. The judge takes care not to kill him. That is the detail Eusebius keeps returning to. The whole apparatus is arranged so that he will break rather than die, because a dead Origen is a martyr and a broken one is an argument.
suggested_refs: The Decian libelli, certificates of sacrifice, surviving in the Egyptian papyri

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, out alive and writing letters
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI, reports the survival and the consolatory letters written afterwards; no recantation is recorded and no sentence survives. The physical consequences of the imprisonment are not stated by any ancient source, and the common assumption that the torture killed him is not attested. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Decius dies on campaign in 251 and the persecution stops with him. Origen comes out alive, sixty-six years old, having said nothing the court wanted. He writes letters afterwards to console other people, and Eusebius, who read them, calls them full of help for those in need of it. What the year in irons did to his body no source states, and the assumption that it killed him rests on nothing anyone wrote down. To the churches that never accepted his deposition he is now a confessor.
suggested_refs: The third-century category of the confessor, the Christian who suffered without being executed

stops.name: Tyre, the sixty-ninth year
stops.date_confidence: reported, and the pool's date corrected. Jerome, De Viris Illustribus 54, anchors the death to the reign of Gallus and Volusianus, who were killed in August 253, so the pool's 253/254 overshoots; Wikipedia's biography has him dying less than a year after his release in 251, which would push it earlier. Give c. 251-253. Wikipedia further calls the Tyre burial 'a later legend, recounted by Jerome and numerous itineraries', to which 'little value can be attached', so the tag is reported, not attested. Coordinates are the Tyre pin already in use in this corpus. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Jerome supplies the only ending anyone has: a reign, an age, a city. Gallus and Volusianus were killed in August 253, so the anchor will not stretch past that summer, and other reckonings put him dead within a year of walking out of prison. He was never executed and he was never canonised. Later travellers to Tyre were shown a tomb said to be his; later scholars have declined to attach any value to that tradition. No grave has been identified, then or since.
stops.quote: He lived until the time of Gallus and Volusianus, that is, until his sixty-ninth year, and died at Tyre, in which city he also was buried.
stops.quote_source: Jerome, De Viris Illustribus 54, tr. NPNF2
sources: Wikipedia, 'Origen', on the value of the Tyre tradition
suggested_refs: The medieval pilgrim itineraries that report a shown tomb of Origen at Tyre

stops.name: Constantinople, the edict to Mennas
stops.date_confidence: attested to 543, sometimes given as 542 or 544 (Wikipedia, 'Origen', legacy section; Justinian's Letter to Mennas). A home synod at Constantinople endorsed the condemnation the same year. Month and day are ordering devices. The stop is a posthumous event concerning Origen and his books, not a place he went.
stops.campa: Three centuries after his death the emperor Justinian issues a theological edict addressed to the patriarch Mennas, condemning Origen by name and ordering his writings burned, and a synod sitting in the city endorses it inside the year. The charges are the pre-existence of souls and the restoration of all things at the end, both of them propositions he had put in the book where he marked off which questions the apostolic teaching had settled and which it had left open. By 543 the Greek of that book was already scarce, and what circulated under his name included material his defenders said was not his.
suggested_refs: Justinian's edict to Mennas and the nine anathemas appended to it

stops.name: Constantinople, the eleventh anathema
stops.date_confidence: contested and not resolved. The Second Council of Constantinople sat from 5 May to 2 June 553. The fifteen anathemas against Origen popularly attributed to it do not appear in the surviving acts of its eight sessions and no debate on them is recorded there; critical scholarship assigns them to a separate pre-conciliar home synod. Origen's name does appear in the council's eleventh general anathema in most of the manuscript tradition. Wikipedia states the council 'may have anathematized Origen, or it may have only condemned certain heretical teachings which claimed to be derived from Origen'. The existing justinian_i.journey.json stop for this council covers the Three Chapters business only.
stops.campa: The Fifth Ecumenical Council sits for eight sessions in the spring of 553. Fifteen anathemas against Origen are popularly attributed to it, and the surviving acts of those eight sessions contain neither the fifteen anathemas nor any recorded debate about them; critical scholarship assigns them to a separate synod held just before. What the council's own text does carry, in most of the manuscript tradition, is his name in the eleventh anathema, in a list of heretics. Whether the council condemned the man or only the teachings that travelled under his name is still argued from those same manuscripts.
sources: Acts of the Second Council of Constantinople, 553
Wikipedia, 'Origen', on the disputed fifteen anathemas
justinian_i.journey.json, Second Council of Constantinople stop
suggested_refs: The fifteen anathemas against Origen, whose conciliar status is a live textual dispute

stops.name: Tura, the quarry tunnels
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1941 (Brent Nongbri, 'The Tura Papyri'). The pool's coordinate of 29.9394, 31.2864 sits about three kilometres west of Tura, down at the riverside rather than at the limestone quarries in the hills where the cache was found; the coordinate is corrected here to the town's own point. The day within August is not recorded.
stops.campa: Workmen clearing rubble from the limestone quarry tunnels at Tura, south of Cairo, in the August of 1941, come on a hidden cache of papyrus codices. Inside it are Greek works of Origen that had been lost entirely: the Dialogue with Heraclides, the treatise On the Passover, fragments of Against Celsus, and fragments of the commentary on Romans. The find scattered almost at once. Part went to the Bodmer Foundation by way of a Cairo collection in 1953, and ten further leaves surfaced in an attic in New England in the 1980s.
suggested_refs: The Tura codices, dispersed across the Bodmer Foundation, Cairo, and several private hands

stops.name: Munich, twenty-nine homilies in a Byzantine hand
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2012 for the identification by Marina Molin Pradel at the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, with Lorenzo Perrone's Greek critical edition in 2015 and Joseph W. Trigg's English translation in 2021 (Catholic University of America Press, publisher's page for Homilies on the Psalms). Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: An archivist at the Bavarian State Library, Marina Molin Pradel, is cataloguing a twelfth-century Byzantine codex, Monacensis Graecus 314, when she recognises the voice in it. The manuscript holds twenty-nine homilies on the Psalms, in Greek, by Origen, unknown to every previous list. A critical edition follows in 2015 and an English translation in 2021. Preaching taken down by shorthand writers in a Palestinian harbour town in the 240s, copied out by a Byzantine scribe nine hundred years later and shelved unread in Bavaria for another nine hundred, is read again.
sources: Catholic University of America Press, Homilies on the Psalms (cuapress.org/9780813233192/homilies-on-the-psalms/)
suggested_refs: Codex Monacensis Graecus 314, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek
Lorenzo Perrone's 2015 Greek critical edition in the GCS series
